text: No PSI experiment burned solid materials inside the lunar habitat atmosphere: solid-fuel flight tests (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire I-III) ran at 13.6-22.2 % oxygen near sea-level pressure, while the habitat is planned at 30-34 % oxygen and 56.5-70.3 kPa. Results for these materials are a lower bound on how easily things will burn.

Outside PSI, drop-tower centrifuge tests found some materials burn at lower oxygen in lunar gravity than on Earth (Mylar film about 5.75 points lower, Ultem and Nomex 2-3 points lower), so 1 g flammability screening is not automatically conservative on the Moon.

The PSI tests closest to the habitat's oxygen level are gas flames - the Burning Rate Emulator (21-40 % O2), cool flames (up to 85 %) and spherical flames (up to 30 %) - plus FLEX droplets (up to 34 %). They speak to oxygen-rich burning but not to cabin materials.

Same atmosphere as the lunar habitat, in a much smaller volume: in Saffire IV-VI, 1.5-3.2 kW fires in 17-19 m3 raised temperature only near the fire but pushed CO and CO2 past crew limits, and a typical smoke alarm level came only after 981 s. In a rover cabin the gases build up faster.
No PSI solid-material test covers 30-34 % oxygen at 56.5-70.3 kPa; BASS-II flow limits (quenching vs blowoff) are the best guide for how cabin ventilation changes flammability.

The Mars habitat atmosphere is assumed equal to the lunar habitat here; no PSI data exist at Mars gravity. Drop-tower tests at 0.38 g found Nomex and Mylar burning at 3.1-3.35 points lower oxygen than in 1 g.
Microgravity and 1 g results do not always bound intermediate gravity: for the three materials tested, the lowest oxygen limit was at lunar or Martian gravity, not at either end.

The ISS atmosphere (21 % O2, 101.3 kPa, microgravity) is where PSI is strongest: BASS, BASS-II and Saffire burned fabrics and plastics at these conditions, SAME and SAME-R measured smoke, and FLEX studied suppression by CO2 and helium.

In microgravity, ventilation decides flammability: BASS-II found a window of air speed in which PMMA keeps burning - too little flow quenches the flame, too much blows it off - and Saffire-II found thin silicone that burns on Earth does not sustain burning in 0 g.
Orion is assumed to carry ISS cabin air, so the ISS evidence applies: large-scale Saffire fires in Cygnus are the closest analogue for a fire in a crew vehicle of similar size.

Pure oxygen at 29.6 kPa is far outside every PSI envelope except the inverse gas flames (oxidizer up to 85 % O2). Apollo 1 showed how fast cabin materials burn in pure oxygen; no PSI experiment tested suit materials.
